In This Video

Peptic Ulcer Disease

Definition

Causes

Clinical features

Diagnosis

Regulation of HCl secretion and treatment of PUD

Definition

Peptic ulcer literally means ulcer caused by digestive enzymes

Peptic ulcer disease is characterized by discontinuation in the inner lining of the gastrointestinal tract (usually occur in the stomach or proximal duodenum, it may involve lower esophagus, distal duodenum or jejunum)

Causes

Peptic ulcer occur due to imbalance between local invasive factor (amount of HCl acid produced) and the protective mechanisms (mucus production and bicarbonate secretion by the gastric mucosa)

The most common causes being H. Pylori associated PUD and NSAID associated PUD

H. Pylori associated PUD

Most common cause of PUD

H. pylori is a gram negative bacilli that is found within the gastric epithelial cells

This bacteria is responsible for 90% of duodenal ulcers and 70-90 % of gastric ulcer, it is commonly acquired in childhood

H. Pylori has multiple different virulence factors allowing it to adhere and inflame gastric mucosa and impairs bicarbonate secretion (it destroys the defensive mechanisms)

Virulence factors include:

Urease: H. pylori secretes urease to break down urea into ammonia which protect the organism by neutralizing the gastric acid

Toxins: H. pylori also secretes toxins that lead to mucosal inflammation and tissue damage

Flagella: H. pylori has flagella that provide motility and allow movement towards the gastric epithelium through the mucus layer

NSAID associated PUD

Second most common cause of PUD

Prostaglandin secretion work to decrease amount of HCl produced by the parietal cells and it work to thickens the mucus layer protecting the mucosa

NSAIDs work to block the prostaglandin synthesis by inhibiting COX 1 enzyme leading to high HCl secretion and less mucus production and it also lead to decrease gastric mucosal blood flow resulting in PUD

Other medications causing PUD

Corticosteroids

Bisphosphonates

Potassium chloride

Fluorouracil

Smoking and Alcohol may lead to PUD

Smoking may lead to duodenal ulcers

Alcohol can irritate gastric mucosa and increase acidity

Other causes of PUD

Zollinger-Ellison syndrome: gastrinoma

Malignancy (gastric/lung cancer, lymphomas)

Stress (Acute illness, burns, head injury): increase acid secretion

Vascular insufficiency: less blood = less mucus production

Radiation therapy: direct injury

Crohn disease

Chemotherapy

Clinical features

Epigastric pain usually occurs within 15-30 min following a meal in patients with gastric ulcer, while in patients with duodenal ulcer the pain tend to occur 2-3 hours after a meal

Patient also may experience bloating, abdominal fullness, nausea and vomiting, weight loss/gain, hematemesis and melena

Warning (Alarm) symptoms that require urgent referral and EGD testing include:

  • Unintentional weight loss
  • Progressive dysphagia
  • Overt gastrointestinal bleeding
  • Iron deficiency anemia
  • Recurrent emesis
  • Family history of upper GI malignancy

Diagnosis

History and physical examination

EGD: gold standard and most accurate test to diagnose gastric and duodenal ulcer; American society of GI endoscopy recommends EGD evaluation for patients over 50 years of age and new onset of dyspeptic symptoms; also recommends EGD evaluation for all patients present with alarm symptoms

Contrast swallow (indicated when EGD is contraindicated)

CBC: to look for infections

LFT: to check for liver disease

Amylase and lipase: pancreatic disease

Serum gastrin level: if Zollinger Ellison syndrome is suspected

H. Pylori testing

H. Pylori testing

Serologic testing

Urea breath test: high sensitivity and specificity

Antibodies to H. pylori levels

Stool antigen test and urine ELISA and rapid urine test

Endoscopic biopsy

PUD Treatment

Treatment of PUD is done through returning the balance between local invasive factor (amount of HCl acid produced) and the protective mechanisms (mucus production and bicarbonate secretion by the gastric mucosa)

So this is done by either decreasing the local invasive factor (decreasing HCl acid secretion) or by strengthening the defensive mechanisms

To understand how the local invasive factors are reduced, first we have to understand how the HCl acid secretion is regulated

Drugs that neutralize HCl: antacids

Drugs that decrease HCl secretion (Antisecretory drugs)

H2 blockers: cimetidine, ranitidine, famotidine

Proton pump inhibitors: omeprazole, lansoprazole …

PPI have largely replaced H2 receptor blockers due to their superior efficacy

Drugs that increase mucosal defense mechanisms:

  • PGE1 analogues: misoprostol
  • Sucralfate
  • Colloid bismuth compounds: e.g. bismuth subcitrate
  • Carbenoxolone

Treatment for H. Pylori infection: PPI + Antibiotics

Refractory cases require surgery

Life style modifications

Stop smoking, spicy food, alcohol, coffee and tea : because they increase HCl

Avoid stress: because it elevates HCl

Avoid medication that promote ulcer formation: e.g. NSAIDs

Regulation of HCl secretion

Stomach contain gastric glands which contain multiple types of cells including parietal cells (secretes HCl), chief cells (secreting pepsin), G cells (secreting gastrin), enterochromaffin cells (secreting histamine)

Histamine is the main activator of the parietal cells to secrete HCl

Parietal cell has many receptors, including M1 receptor, G receptor, H2 receptor and prostaglandin receptor

Any stimulation to the M1, G, H2 receptor lead to increase HCl secretion from the parietal cell

While stimulating the prostaglandin receptor would lead to decrease HCl secretion

Stimulating M1, G receptors would give a weak stimulation to HCl secretion from the parietal cell compared to H2 stimulation which gives powerful stimulation leading to a lot of acid secretion

Vagal stimulation from the myenteric plexus would increase acetylcholine levels leading to simulation of M1 receptors on parietal cells, but not just that; it also stimulate the g cells to produce more gastrin which work on the enterochromaffin cells to secrete histamine which go back to bind to the parietal cells giving powerful stimulation to acid secretion

Now stimulating the H2 receptors on the parietal cells lead to increase cAMP levels => activation of many protein kinases inside the cell => break down of H2CO3 into hydrogen and bicarb

Hydrogen exit into the stomach lumen by the H/K ATPase (proton pump)

Hydrogen bind to Cl in the lumen to form HCl

Prostaglandin antagonizes this cycle by decreasing cAMP and decreasing HCl secretion

Prostaglandin also responsible for protective mucus production and bicarbonate secretion

Prostaglandin also responsible for vasodilatation to increase blood flow to the stomach => ulcer heals faster
